en: The Auspicious Śārīrakādhikaraṇaratnamālā with its Commentary (Prakāśa)
The first quarter of the first chapter: Illumination.
[Salutation to] Him whose chest is made fragrant by the incomparable scent of the musk-paste applied to Śrī’s breasts.
May the auspiciousness of my dwelling, marked by the Kaustubha gem, spread forth.

May this faultless pearl necklace, composed of the succession of my gurus and strung with the jewels of the traditional teachings (āmnāya) of the lords among ascetics, Nātha and Yamuna, shine within my heart. [This was written] by the grace of Śrīnivāsa, the preceptor of the Kauśika lineage.
Having composed this *Adhikaraṇaratnamālā*, he has explained it.

The Blessed Bādarāyaṇa, being supremely compassionate and desiring to favor those seeking liberation (mumukṣu), composed the Śārīraka-śāstra—which consists of the investigation of that [Self]—with the intent to determine, through the inquiry into various forms of knowledge (vidyā), that specific deity who is heard of in the higher knowledges as the one to be worshipped by seekers of liberation.
He did so because he perceived that, due to the corruption of this very scripture by later commentators, there was a lack of attainment of its purpose for the sake of introducing the teaching.

The author of this work, desiring to compose a compendium of the meaning of the extensive and profound *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya*— which was composed by the venerable commentator (*bhāṣyakṛt*) who sought to establish its purposefulness through an exposition of the intent of the original author of the treatise as it truly stands— and wishing to perform daily worship of his supreme deity, begins the work titled *Śārīrakādhikaraṇaratnamālā*. At the outset, for the sake of the unimpeded completion of the work he intends to compose, [he offers praise to] the *Śārīrakaśāstra*...
He performs an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) consisting of the worship of the Supreme Deity as definitively determined.

Here, by the word "resplendent" (*ujjvalam*) in the phrase "on the peak of the glorious Śeṣa-mountain," a particular incarnation is established; and since that [incarnation] serves the purpose of being one's own refuge, and especially because its specific placement of the hand suggests that his own foot is to be resorted to, his abiding as the means (*upāya*) is indicated. By the phrase "blazing on the lap of the Lord of Serpents," [it is shown that] in the supreme world of Vaikuṇṭha, Janārdana, accompanied by Śrī, is the Great Yogin...

By the method described in such passages as, "The Sustainer of the World [sits] upon a divine lion-throne, provided with a divine carpet and adorned by the jewels on the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa," a particular type of seat situated above Ananta—who is eternally present—is intended to be expressed. And by that, his abiding there as an object of enjoyment for the liberated ones is made known. Thus, by this...

By means of these two adjectives, the status of Śrīnivāsa, the Blessed One, as both the means (*upāya*) in the realm of sport (*līlāvibhūti*) and the goal (*upeya*) in the eternal realm (*nityavibhūti*) is indicated; thus, what was established in the chapters on the means and the fruit (*sādhanaphalādhyāya*) of the *Śārīraka-śāstra* is here suggested. [He is] radiant upon the crest of the Supreme Veda (*nigamottamāṅga*).

By this, the authority for both [positions] has been demonstrated therein. For in the *Subālopaniṣad* and other Upaniṣads, it is traditionally taught that Śrīnivāsa possesses both the nature of the means (*upāyatva*) and the nature of the goal (*upeyatva*), through such passages as: "The mother, the father, the brother, the dwelling, the refuge, the friend, and the final resort—Nārāyaṇa. In that context, the term "refuge" (*śaraṇam*) denotes his nature as the means, while the term "final resort" (*gatiḥ*) denotes his nature as the goal.

Now, following the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-vicāra*), because ritual action has thus been investigated, the remaining duty is that one should desire to know Brahman (*brahma-jijñāsā*), which is the object of that desire. This is the sense.
To explain this meaning, the following verse was composed:

"I worship that Brahman known as Śrīnivāsa, who is the object of inquiry for those persons who, having performed the investigation of ritual action (*karma-vicāra*), have ceased their longing for the fruits of action and seek the human goal of liberation (*mokṣa-puruṣārtha*)."

The state (*bhāva*) of a person who has studied the Vedas is as follows: when, through the logic set forth in Jaimini’s *Karmamīmāṃsā*, there arises the certainty that the nature of rituals such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* is of this kind, that it must be performed in this manner, and that its fruit, consisting of heaven and so forth, is of such a nature; then, because of the knowledge that fruits such as heaven are perishable, the desire for their attainment ceases. Since there exists an initial impression (*āpātapratīti*) regarding the human goal of liberation (*mokṣa*), which consists in attaining [Brahman], the desire for its attainment arises. Thus, when the desire for the attainment of Brahman has arisen, [one realizes] that the nature of Brahman is of this kind.

And this [means] for attaining that, as well as the fruit consisting of the attainment of that—being of such a nature and so forth—is determined by the principles (nyāya) stated in the Brahma-mīmāṃsā; that which is to be thus determined is the Brahman named Śrīnivāsa, whom one propitiates through the chanting of His names, service at His feet, circumambulation, prostration, and other such acts.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) is found in the *Arthavāda* section of the *Karmamīmāṃsā* within these two sūtras: "Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless; therefore, they are said to be non-eternal," and "But because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, the [arthavādas] must exist for the purpose of praise. This is because there is a rule that the Veda in general must convey some kind of duty to be performed (*kartavya*), and thus, for those [passages] that convey a duty to be performed...

Having established the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the first sūtra—that because the authority of Vedic sentences in the form of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is impossible, there is no rule of authority for the Veda as a whole—Jaimini established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the subsequent sūtra: even though explanatory passages lack the capacity to convey meaning through some specific duty to be performed, their authority is indeed established by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunctive sentence, as they convey excellence (*prāśastya*) connected to the action prescribed by the proximate injunctive sentence.

And this is logical: for the ignorant, the apprehension of word-meaning (*śaktigraha*) first occurs through the linguistic usage of elders. For example, when a certain person proficient in language says "Bring the cow" to another who is not so proficient, the man directed by him brings the cow. Then again, when it is said "Take the cow," he takes it elsewhere. A bystander, being ignorant, having observed the bringing of the cow and the taking of the cow following those two successive utterances of the sentence, understands that the man directed by him possessed the cognition of the duty to bring the cow [upon hearing] "Bring the cow."

Determined that the knowledge of the cow’s duty to be led arises from the sentence and specifically from the subsequent sentence "Lead the cow," [the cognizer concludes]: because the word *go* (cow) conveys an object capable of being connected with two actions—namely, leading and [the act of] bringing—it denotes the cow; the word *ānaya* (bring) denotes the action of bringing; and the word *naya* (lead) denotes the action of leading. Thus, regarding those respective words...

One grasps the *śakti* (denotative power). Likewise, through other sentences used by elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), one comes to know the *śakti* of various words in their respective meanings. Thus, when the grasp of *śakti* arises solely from linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), and because it is observed that all such usage is directed toward an object to be accomplished (*kārya-artha-paratva*), one concludes that all words are directed toward some object to be accomplished. Therefore, in accordance with the process of learning the language (*vyutpatti*), all words indeed have as their purport an object to be accomplished. Thus [it is established] regarding worldly [usage].

Since it has been established that words have action as their primary purport, according to the maxim "those very same words used in common parlance are the same as those used in the Veda," even Vedic words must likewise have action as their purport.

Consequently, because the Upanishadic sentences lack any intended meaning directed toward Brahman— which is not of the nature of action— the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra, which consists of an inquiry into the Upanishads, need not be commenced.
The established conclusion—

that the first acquisition of linguistic usage by children arises solely from the linguistic behavior of elders— is contrary to the experience of everyone, since the first acquisition of usage is established by experience as occurring in quite another way.

For example, parents and others, desiring to instruct their own children, point to objects such as the moon, a cow, or [other relatives] like a father or maternal uncle, and repeatedly employ words such as "this is the moon," "this is a cow," "this is a father," or "this is a maternal uncle," preceded by the pointing of a finger. And the child, through the observation of the constant concomitance (*sāhacarya*) between the pointing of the finger toward the object present before them and the employment of those respective words, [understands the relationship].

By means of an awakening stimulus (udbodhaka), one recalls that in such a type of activity, there was a cognition of the relationship between those specific words and those specific meanings experienced in a previous birth. Then, knowing in a general way that some relationship exists between words such as "moon" and objects such as the moon present before him, and hearing many people using those words for those respective objects, and further knowing that no other possible relationship between the word and its meaning is feasible, [one concludes]: "This word is the indicator of this meaning. Thus, regarding those two...

[The opponent] determines a specific relation consisting of the nature of the relationship between the object of cognition (*bodhya*) and the cognizer (*bodhaka*). Thus, since it is observed that the apprehension of the word-potency (*śakti*) of words occurs first with respect to an object not yet connected to an action (*kārya*), it is established that the apprehension of potency occurs first with respect to an object connected to an action, based on the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).

Furthermore, the claim that the apprehension of potency arises only from sentences directed toward an action (*kāryapara-vākya*) is untenable; for even from sentences directed toward an accomplished fact (*siddhārtha*), such as "Caitra, a son has been born to you," [the apprehension of potency occurs].

Because the apprehension of the expressive power [of words] is observed. For instance, when someone commissioned by Caitra to announce the birth of his son addresses Caitra with the sentence, "Caitra, a son has been born to you," a certain person who is unacquainted with the meaning observes that a son has indeed been born to Caitra in his house, that the man was commissioned to inform him of it, and that Caitra’s face brightens upon hearing those words. Thus, he determines that the sentence uttered toward Caitra possesses the capacity to convey the meaning consisting of the birth of a son to Caitra.

Therefore, there is no rule that the apprehension of word-meaning (*śaktigraha*) occurs only from sentences directed toward an action (*kāryapara*). Thus, since the apprehension of meaning occurs appropriately—sometimes from sentences directed toward an established entity (*siddhapara*) regarding what is not connected to an action, and sometimes from sentences directed toward an action regarding the action itself—the Prābhākara claim that all words have as their purport only the meaning of an action (*kāryārtha*) is devoid of reason. Consequently, because it is possible for Vedānta sentences to have their primary purport (*tātparya*) upon Brahman as an established reality (*siddharūpa*), the treatise consisting of the inquiry into that [Brahman] ought to be commenced.

The fact that this Sūtra is intent upon refuting such a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is ascertained precisely from its demonstration that Brahman, which is an established entity (siddhavastu) not connected to an action (kārya), is the subject of inquiry. For if all Vedānta passages were intent upon [injunctions of] action, then the description of Brahman—an established form—as the object of inquiry by means of the Vedānta passages would be impossible.

[If it is argued that] this would be untenable, and that there would thus be a contradiction with the reasoning of Jaimini cited previously, it is replied: Jaimini refuted [the objection] by accepting the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that all Vedic sentences have *kārya* (what is to be done) as their primary purport; however, that was not his actual intention. Thus, there is no contradiction between the two. In this verse, by the phrase "by those who have composed the inquiry into action" (*viracitakarmavicāraiḥ*), it is established through a specific qualification of the person that the inquiry into the Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) must be undertaken immediately after the inquiry into action; therefore, with respect to the inquiry into the Brahman—

The fact that the inquiry into action (*karmavicāra*) invariably precedes [the inquiry into Brahman] is thus established. If it is asked why this is so, it is said: when a person who has studied the Vedas perceives, upon a superficial reading of Vedic passages, that the fruit of ritual action is in some cases stable while in others it is unstable, a desire arises to determine which of these two is the ultimate reality. Consequently, for a person engaged in those scriptures that provide such determination, [an inquiry into the means of attaining] the fruits of action [is required].

First, engagement occurs in the inquiry into the scriptures (*śāstra-vicāra*) alone; for, due to beginningless latent impressions (*anādi-vāsanā*), one is certain that ritual actions (*karma*) are easy to perform, whereas one is certain that the knowledge of Brahman (*brahma-jñāna*), being unpracticed, is difficult to attain. Since it is impossible to engage in a laborious means when the desired goal can be accomplished through an easier means, there is an obstruction to engaging in the inquiry into Brahman—which is the means for determining its fruit—due to the desire to determine the fruits of ritual actions. Once the inquiry into karma has been performed, the certainty arises that the fruits of karma are unstable. For example:

In the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) within the *Karmakāṇḍa*, it is heard [in scripture]: "One should sacrifice with the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice. Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether some distinct sacrifice named Dākṣāyaṇa is being enjoined, or whether some accessory (*guṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices themselves is being enjoined. On this point, the great sage Jaimini, by means of the aphorism "Or it is a modification, because of the context" (*vikāro vā prakaraṇāt*), establishes that the meaning of the scriptural statement is that a repetition of the New and Full Moon sacrifices must be performed for the sake of increasing the fruit, such as heaven.

Thus it is concluded. By this, the certainty arises that the results of rituals such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, namely heaven (*svarga*) and so forth, are perishable. For if the results of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites—such as heaven—were eternal, then the injunction for the repeated performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* for the sake of its persistence over a long period would be rendered useless. Thus, once the certainty regarding the impermanence of the fruits of ritual action is established, the obstacle consisting of the desire to investigate ritual action is removed, and an inclination toward investigating the Veda (*brāhmaṇa*), driven by the desire for that investigation, comes into being.
The inquiry into Brahman necessarily depends upon the inquiry into ritual action.

Let this be so. However, it may be asked: since this verse is composed for the purpose of elucidating the intention of the Sūtra, how can the statement that the Brāhmaṇa is named Śrīnivāsa—which is not touched upon in the Sūtra—be justified? To this it is replied: In this treatise on the Mīmāṃsā of the Brāhmaṇa, having first proposed that the Brāhmaṇa is the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*), and having stated His definition (*lakṣaṇa*) as being the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe, [the subsequent sections] proceed toward the application of that definition to the definiendum and its exclusion from all other things.

In the sections beginning with the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*, having identified the Great Person Śrīnivāsa—well-known from the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, the *Subālopaniṣad*, and other sources—by means of His unique specific attributes, and having demonstrated the application of the definition to Him and its exclusion from others, it is established that He alone is intended by the Sūtrakāra as the referent of the word *brahman*. Therefore, here too, in the first Sūtra, it is He who is intended by the word *brahman*; thus, He is not untouched by the words of the Sūtras.
This will be clarified further below; thus, everything is faultless.
Thus concludes the section concerning the desire to know (Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa) || 1 ||
